31 An oil drop of mass 2.6  10–15
kg and with a charge of – 4.8  10–19
C is in a vacuum between two
horizontal plates. The plates have a separation of 2.0 cm and a potential difference (p.d.) between
them of 1200 V, as shown.
+1200 V
plates
oil drop
2.0 cm
0 V
Which statement describes the motion of the oil drop?
A
It is stationary.
B
It has a downward acceleration of 9.7 m s–2.
C
It has an upward acceleration of 1.3 m s–2.
D
It has an upward acceleration of 11 m s–2.

hints: Notice the top plate is $+1200 \text{ V}$ and the bottom plate is $0 \text{ V}$ with separation $2.0 \text{ cm}$, so calculate the uniform field strength $E = V/d$ and its downward direction.
Compare the two vertical forces on the drop: weight $mg$ downward and electric force $|q|E$ upward because the charge $-4.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ is negative.
Use Newton's second law with the small difference between those two forces: $a = (|q|E - mg)/m$ with upward taken as positive.
walkthrough: Find the electric field between the horizontal plates: $E = V/d = 1200 / 0.020 = 60000 \text{ V m}^{-1}$. The field points downward from $+1200 \text{ V}$ to $0 \text{ V}$.
Find the electric force magnitude: $F_E = |q|E = 4.8 \times 10^{-19} \times 60000 = 2.88 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$. Because the charge is negative, the force is opposite to the field, so upward.
Find the weight: $W = mg = 2.6 \times 10^{-15} \times 9.81 = 2.55 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$ downward.
Find the resultant force upward: $F_{net} = F_E - W = 2.88 \times 10^{-14} - 2.55 \times 10^{-14} = 0.33 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$ upward.
Find the acceleration: $a = F_{net}/m = 0.33 \times 10^{-14} / 2.6 \times 10^{-15} \approx 1.3 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ upward. This is option C

A.explanation: The electric force is slightly larger than the weight, so the forces do not balance and the drop is not stationary.

B.explanation: The electric force on the negative drop is upward and almost balances weight, so the net force cannot be almost full weight downward.

C.explanation: Upward electric force exceeds downward weight by a small amount, giving a net upward force and an acceleration of about $1.3 \text{m s}^{-2}$.

D.explanation: This adds the full electric acceleration to $g$, but weight acts downward so it must be subtracted from the upward electric force.
